plants.name: Camellia japonica
plants.description: Glossy evergreen shrubs and small trees light up the coldest weeks of the year with rose-like blooms. Crimson petals surround a boss of golden stamens, and bright flowers stand out against dark, leathery leaves, sometimes with snow nearby.
plants.bloomingSeason: Wild plants flower from about January to March, so January 19 falls within the season.
plants.location: Coastal woodlands and gardens of Japan, including the southern and western regions
plants.funFact: Camellias are closely related to the tea plant, Camellia sinensis. In Japan, the camellia's seeds are pressed into tsubaki oil, which has long been used for hair care and for polishing wood and blades.

plants.name: Agapanthus praecox
plants.commonName: African lily, Lily of the Nile
plants.description: Rounded globes of trumpet-shaped flowers sit on tall, sturdy stems above arching, strap-like leaves. In midsummer they bring cool blue to sunny borders, roadsides and coastal gardens.
plants.bloomingSeason: Peak flowering runs from about November to February in the Southern Hemisphere, which covers mid-January.
plants.location: Native to South Africa and widely grown in the summer gardens of Australia
plants.funFact: Despite the common name, it is not a true lily. The genus name comes from the Greek words for 'love' and 'flower'. It thrives in heat and thick, fleshy roots store water to survive dry spells.

plants.name: Helleborus niger
plants.description: Nodding, saucer-shaped white flowers with a crown of yellow stamens push up through frost and leaf litter when almost nothing else is awake. They fade to soft pink as they age.
plants.bloomingSeason: Flowers from December through the winter months, so it is typically in bloom on January 19, especially in mild winters.
plants.location: Mountain woodlands of the Alps and central and southern Europe, as well as cold-season gardens across the Northern Hemisphere
plants.funFact: Its name 'niger' (black) refers to its dark roots, not its flowers. The showy 'petals' are actually sepals that stay on the plant for weeks, which keeps the display going long after a normal petal would have dropped.
